```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  prompt = FALSE
)
source_roots <- c(".", "..")
source_roots <- source_roots[
  file.exists(file.path(source_roots, "DESCRIPTION"))
]
if (length(source_roots) && requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(
    source_roots[[1L]],
    quiet = TRUE,
    export_all = FALSE
  )
} else {
  library(readPBOC)
}

package_file <- function(...) {
  pieces <- c(...)
  relative <- do.call(file.path, as.list(pieces))
  candidates <- c(
    file.path(source_roots, "inst", relative),
    system.file(..., package = "readPBOC")
  )
  found <- candidates[
    nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates) & !dir.exists(candidates)
  ]
  if (!length(found)) stop("Could not find packaged file ", paste(pieces, collapse = "/"))
  normalizePath(found[[1L]], winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
}

html_fixture <- package_file("extdata", "readpboc-table-fixture.html")
```

`readPBOC` reads public PBOC pages and attachments. It does not implement an
authenticated API: no username, password, token, cookie, or environment
credential is required. The package uses fixed official HTTPS endpoints for
discovery and follows attachment URLs returned by those pages.

## What is contacted, and what is stored

The discovery functions (`pboc_years()`, `pboc_sections()`,
`pboc_catalog()`, and `pboc_releases()`) make HTTPS requests to the official
Chinese or English indexes. `pboc_read()` makes a temporary download when its
input is a remote spreadsheet or HTML URL, reads it, and removes that
temporary file after the call. A remote PDF is not parsed: use
`pboc_download()`
to retain the official PDF as an explicit local side effect.

There is no persistent cache, startup download, home-directory write, or
credential store. The functions that intentionally write files are:

* `pboc_download()`,
  which creates the requested destination directory, preserves each
  attachment, and writes a CSV manifest by default; and
* `pboc_snapshot()`,
  which writes the catalog CSV path supplied by the caller.

Use `tempdir()` in examples and tests when a durable artifact is not the goal.

## Timeouts, retries, and user agents

The default HTTP timeout is 60 seconds. Discovery and release-page fetches make
up to three total attempts for transport failures, server errors, or HTTP 429,
with a short increasing backoff. Direct attachment reads and downloads make
one transfer. Other client HTTP errors stop without treating the response as a
successful document. The timeout and user-agent string are ordinary R options:

```{r options}
configured <- local({
  old <- options("readPBOC.timeout", "readPBOC.user_agent")
  on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE)

  options(
    readPBOC.timeout = 30,
    readPBOC.user_agent = "readPBOC-vignette/0.1"
  )
  c(
    timeout = getOption("readPBOC.timeout"),
    user_agent = getOption("readPBOC.user_agent")
  )
})
configured
```

The package does not parallelise requests or require more than one core. Keep
live traversals narrow (`pages = 1L` while exploring), respect the source
server, and save a catalog snapshot when a reproducible run needs a stable
input.

## Offline reading and the PDF boundary

The packaged HTML fixture exercises the local path without a network request.
It is an author-created structural fixture under the package license, not a
PBOC product-data extract. It returns one table when the document has one table
and a list when it has multiple tables. The result carries `source_path` for a
local file; a local path has no remote `source_url`.

```{r local-html}
table <- pboc_read(html_fixture)
stopifnot(is.data.frame(table) || is.list(table))
c(
  class = paste(class(table), collapse = ", "),
  source_path = basename(attr(table, "source_path")),
  source_url = attr(table, "source_url")
)
```

PDFs are deliberately preservation-only. The error is deterministic and is
raised before any PDF parser is invoked:

```{r pdf-error}
pdf_path <- tempfile("readPBOC-", fileext = ".pdf")
file.create(pdf_path)
pdf_message <- tryCatch(
  pboc_read(pdf_path),
  error = function(error) conditionMessage(error)
)
unlink(pdf_path)
pdf_message
```

For a source workbook, use `pboc_read(..., tidy = TRUE)` to obtain the long
form described in the `pboc_tidy()`
reference. HTML parsing is intentionally lighter-weight: it follows the
current table markup and can need maintenance if the official page changes.

## Common failure modes

### The request fails or the site is unavailable

Check the URL and internet connection, then retry a narrow request. A fetch
failure is reported as an error; discovery does not silently return stale
data. The package's short retry policy helps with transient responses but does
not guarantee site availability. If the site is down, use a previously saved
catalog/manifest and work from preserved local files.

### `pboc_data()` reports no matching workbook

The `section` and `item` arguments are regular-expression filters over section
and item labels. Check coverage with `pboc_sections(..., language = "both")`
or `pboc_catalog(..., language = "both")` to inspect Chinese/English
differences. In
`language = "auto"` mode, Chinese is attempted first and English is used only
when the Chinese catalog call errors or has no matching row. An ambiguous
match requires a narrower `item`.

### A table has an unexpected shape or warning

PBOC worksheets are published for human reading and can contain bilingual
headers, repeated tables, notes, or Excel period values. Run
`pboc_tidy()` on a character worksheet read with `col_names = FALSE`; inspect
`value_raw`, `unit`, `source_row`, and `source_column` before applying a
domain-specific conversion. Keep the original workbook with its catalog row.

### The HTML result is empty or has different columns

`pboc_read()` delegates HTML table extraction to `rvest`. Official markup can
change, and a release article is not necessarily a data table. Re-check the
source page and preserve its URL; do not assume that an HTML table has the
same schema as a spreadsheet passed through `pboc_tidy()`.

### The PDF cannot be normalised

This is expected. `readPBOC` does not claim a cross-platform PDF extraction
schema. Use `pboc_download()` to preserve the official file, then choose a
separate PDF workflow appropriate to the document.

## Live calls are opt-in in examples

The following pattern is suitable for an exploratory session but is not run by
CRAN or this offline vignette:

```{r live-pattern, eval=TRUE}
if (interactive()) {
  releases <- pboc_releases(
    language = "en",
    category = "financial_statistics",
    pages = 1L
  )
  if (nrow(releases)) pboc_read_release(releases[1L, , drop = FALSE])
}
```

For deterministic tests, use local fixtures and synthetic catalog frames with
`pboc_revisions()`;
do not make test success depend on live PBOC availability.
